questions.question: The soft cheese Camembert takes its name from a village in which French region?
questions.note: Camembert is named after a hamlet in Normandy, and Camembert de Normandie has held AOC protection since 1983.

questions.question: Which British commander led the allied army that defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
questions.note: Wellington called it 'the nearest-run thing you ever saw', rescued late in the day by Blücher's Prussians.

questions.question: Which large Alpine lake does the River Rhône flow through before heading down into France?
questions.note: The Rhône rises in the Swiss Alps and passes through Lake Geneva before crossing into France towards Lyon.

questions.question: A British car marque later famed for its 'Bentley Boys' took part in the very first 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1923. Which marque?
questions.note: Bentley entered the inaugural Le Mans endurance race in 1923 and went on to win it repeatedly in the 1920s.

questions.question: Which French sculptor created the celebrated bronze 'The Thinker' (Le Penseur)?
questions.note: Rodin conceived The Thinker around 1880 as part of his monumental 'Gates of Hell' before exhibiting it as a standalone work.

questions.question: The English word 'silhouette' comes from the name of which 18th-century French finance minister?
questions.note: His cheap, austere policies as Louis XV's controller-general in 1759 led shadow-profile portraits to be mocked as being done 'à la Silhouette'.

questions.question: In which city on the French island of Corsica was Napoleon Bonaparte born?
questions.note: Ajaccio, the capital of Corsica, was Napoleon's birthplace on 15 August 1769.

questions.question: The medieval 'Auld Alliance', first sealed in 1295, bound France in mutual defence against England with which other country?
questions.note: The France–Scotland pact against a common English enemy endured, on and off, for over 250 years.

questions.question: Gustave Eiffel built the Eiffel Tower as the entrance arch for which 1889 Paris event marking the centenary of the French Revolution?
questions.note: Completed in March 1889, the tower served as the gateway to the Exposition Universelle celebrating 100 years since the Revolution.

questions.question: 'Claret' is the traditional British name for red wine from which French wine region?
questions.note: The British have called red Bordeaux 'claret' since medieval times, when Bordeaux belonged to the English crown through Eleanor of Aquitaine.

questions.question: The Roland-Garros tennis stadium in Paris is named after Roland Garros, a pioneer in what field?
questions.note: Roland Garros made the first flight across the Mediterranean Sea in 1913, and the Paris tennis stadium was named in his honour in 1928.

questions.question: The word 'sabotage' derives from the French 'sabot', which is what kind of footwear?
questions.note: 'Sabot' is a peasant's wooden clog, and 'saboter' meant to work clumsily or noisily, as if in heavy wooden shoes.

questions.question: When a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789, how many prisoners were actually being held inside?
questions.note: The fortress that symbolised royal tyranny held just seven inmates that day, including four forgers and a lone aristocrat.

questions.question: Which town in south-west France is traditionally regarded as the birthplace of the bean-and-meat stew cassoulet?
questions.note: Legend ties the dish to Castelnaudary's defence against Edward the Black Prince during the Hundred Years' War.

questions.question: France won its first football World Cup in 1998, beating which country 3–0 in the final in Paris?
questions.note: France beat defending champions Brazil 3–0 at the Stade de France on 12 July 1998, with Zinedine Zidane scoring twice.

questions.question: Into which body of water does the River Seine flow at Le Havre?
questions.note: The Seine empties into the English Channel (La Manche) at Le Havre, France's largest international shipping port.

questions.question: Which defiant 1960 Édith Piaf song has a title meaning 'No, I regret nothing'?
questions.note: Composed by Charles Dumont, Piaf dedicated her recording to the French Foreign Legion.

questions.question: The word 'chauffeur' comes from the French verb 'chauffer', which means what?
questions.note: Early motor-cars were steam-driven, so a 'chauffeur' was literally a 'stoker' who kept the engine hot before the word came to mean a paid driver.

questions.question: In which year did Napoleon Bonaparte crown himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame?
questions.note: He famously took the crown from Pope Pius VII and placed it on his own head.

questions.question: The Channel Tunnel runs under La Manche from Folkestone in Kent to which French terminal near Calais?
questions.note: The French end of the Channel Tunnel is at Coquelles in the Pas-de-Calais, linked to Folkestone in England.

questions.question: The classic French dessert tarte Tatin is a caramelised upside-down tart made with which fruit?
questions.note: The tart is said to have been created by accident by the Tatin sisters at their hotel in Lamotte-Beuvron.

questions.question: On which British Channel Island did Victor Hugo live in exile and finish 'Les Misérables', at his home Hauteville House?
questions.note: Hugo bought Hauteville House in St Peter Port in 1856 and completed Les Misérables there in 1862 during his exile from Napoleon III's France.

questions.question: The first-ever Winter Olympic Games, held in 1924, took place in which French Alpine town?
questions.note: The 1924 Chamonix Games were the first Winter Olympics, recognised as such retrospectively by the IOC.

questions.question: When the word 'restaurant' first appeared in 18th-century France, what restorative food did it originally refer to?
questions.note: From the French 'restaurer' (to restore), a 'restaurant' was first a fortifying broth before the word came to mean the eating place itself.

questions.question: Which French emperor was captured by the Prussians at the Battle of Sedan in 1870?
questions.note: His surrender toppled the Second Empire and ushered in the Third Republic two days later.

questions.question: In Jules Verne's 'Around the World in Eighty Days', at which London gentlemen's club does Phileas Fogg make his wager to circle the globe?
questions.note: Fogg bets fellow members £20,000 that he can circumnavigate the world in eighty days, setting out with his French valet Passepartout.

questions.question: Cognac brandy is distilled almost entirely from which white grape variety?
questions.note: Ugni Blanc, known in Italy as Trebbiano, accounts for over 98% of the Cognac vineyard.

questions.question: Founded by Greek settlers around 600 BC as Massalia, which Mediterranean port is France's oldest city?
questions.note: Marseille was founded by Greeks from Phocaea around 600 BC as Massalia, making it France's oldest city and its second-largest today.

questions.question: The French Open is the only one of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments played on which court surface?
questions.note: Unlike Wimbledon's grass, the French Open has been contested on outdoor clay courts since 1928, the only Grand Slam to use the surface.

questions.question: In standard French, the number 80 is 'quatre-vingts', which literally means what?
questions.note: French kept a base-20 count of Celtic origin, so 80 is 'four twenties' rather than a distinct word like the Belgian and Swiss 'octante'.
